passages.t: ‘Of first importance’: Christ died, was buried, was raised, appeared
passages.happening:
Paul comes to the heart of the letter. He reminds them of the gospel he preached, which they received, in which they stand, and by which they are saved, if they hold firmly to it (verses 1-2).

“For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve” (verses 3-5).

“After that, He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep” (verse 6). “Then He appeared to James, then to all the apostles” (verse 7). “And last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth” (verse 8).

Paul calls himself the least of the apostles, because he persecuted the church of God (verse 9). “But by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace to me was not in vain” (verse 10). Whether it was he or the others, “this is what we preach, and this is what you believed” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This chapter states the centre of the Christian faith. Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised bodily from the dead on the third day, and appeared to many witnesses. The church has always confessed this. These notes state it as that confession, not as one view among others.

Verses 3 to 5 are not Paul's own words in the first place. He says he ‘received’ them and ‘passed’ them on, the words for handing on a teaching faithfully. He uses the same pair for the Lord's Supper in 11:23. The lines are short and carefully built, four clauses each beginning ‘that’, the way a summary is made to be remembered. They use Peter's Aramaic name, Cephas.

How old is this summary? Paul wrote 1 Corinthians probably in the mid-50s. He had already passed the summary on when he founded the church a few years earlier. And he had received it before that. Scholars of many views, including some who do not believe Jesus rose, treat it as very early. Many date it to within a few years of the crucifixion. Paul tells the Galatians that about three years after his conversion he spent fifteen days in Jerusalem with Cephas and also saw James, the Lord's brother (Galatians 1:18-19), two of the names on this list. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Did the resurrection actually happen?’, sets out this evidence.

The list names witnesses. Cephas. The Twelve. More than five hundred at one time, ‘most of whom are still living’: in effect, go and ask them. James, the brother of Jesus, who had not believed in him during his ministry: “For even His own brothers did not believe in Him” (John 7:5). And last, Paul himself, who met the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3-5).

The list does not name the women who found the tomb empty in the Gospels. Readers have offered reasons, and no one can be sure why.

‘One of untimely birth’ is a harsh phrase, used of a child born dead or too early. Paul uses it of himself. He came late and unready, an enemy of the church. Grace made him an apostle.
passages.ot:
Twice the summary says ‘according to the Scriptures’. It does not name the verses. Christians have long pointed to Isaiah's suffering servant: “But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5). The servant is “assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death” (Isaiah 53:9), and yet afterward “He will see the light of life and be satisfied” (Isaiah 53:11).

For the rising, the first Christians pointed to the psalm Peter quoted at Pentecost: “nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (Psalm 16:10). For the third day, readers point to Hosea, “on the third day He will raise us up” (Hosea 6:2), and to Jonah's three days in the fish, which Jesus himself named as a sign (Matthew 12:40, pointing to Jonah 1:17). Paul's point is that Christ's death and rising were not an accident. They fulfilled what God had said.
passages.asks: Paul calls this the matter ‘of first importance’. Ask what you would name as most important in your faith. Then read verses 3 to 5 slowly, aloud, as the first Christians did. And notice verse 10: if grace could make the church's enemy an apostle, ask what it could make of you.

passages.happening:
“But if it is preached that Christ has been raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” (verse 12).

Paul follows the thought to its end. If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised (verse 13). “And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith” (verse 14). The apostles would be false witnesses about God (verse 15).

“And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins” (verse 17). “Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished” (verse 18). “If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Some in Corinth said ‘there is no resurrection of the dead’. They probably did not deny every kind of life after death. Many Greeks believed the soul lived on, but thought the idea of a dead body being raised was foolish or even unwelcome. When Paul spoke of the resurrection in Athens, “some began to mock him” (Acts 17:32). Some Corinthians may have thought of salvation as the soul's escape from the body.

Paul was a Pharisee, and Pharisees hoped for the resurrection of the dead at the end of the age (Acts 23:6). Paul now says that hope has begun to come true in Christ.

His argument is blunt. The resurrection of Christ and the resurrection of believers stand or fall together. If the dead are not raised, Christ was not raised. And if Christ was not raised, everything falls: the preaching, the faith, the forgiveness of sins, the hope for those who have died.

Few faiths name the fact that would sink them. This one does. Paul does not say faith is useful even if it is not true. He says that if Christ was not raised, Christians are to be pitied. The site's Honest Answers on the resurrection and on ‘What if Christianity is wrong?’ take this up.
passages.ot:
The hope of resurrection grew in the Old Testament. Job said, “Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God” (Job 19:26). Isaiah promised, “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19). Daniel foresaw it most plainly: “And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2).

A psalm trusted God beyond the grave: “But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself” (Psalm 49:15). Sheol is the Old Testament's name for the place of the dead.
passages.hard:
Does it matter whether the resurrection really happened, as long as its message inspires people?

Paul says it does, and these notes say so with him. The church confesses that Jesus was raised bodily from the dead as an event in history, on a particular day, in a particular city, with a tomb left empty and witnesses who saw him. It is not a picture of hope or a way of saying his teaching lives on. The historic creeds confess it: the Nicene Creed confesses that on the third day he rose again. It belongs to the floor of the Christian faith.

Paul is honest about what follows if it is false: ‘your faith is futile’. That honesty is part of why the claim can be weighed. A thoughtful skeptic can look at the evidence and still not believe. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Did the resurrection actually happen?’, sets out the case against at full strength and the case for.
passages.asks: Paul stakes everything on one event. Ask what your faith actually rests on: a feeling, a habit, a community, or a risen Lord. And if you have doubts about the resurrection, ask whether you have looked at the evidence for yourself.

passages.t: ‘Christ the firstfruits’, and ‘God all in all’
passages.happening:
“But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (verse 20).

“For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man. For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive” (verses 21-22). But each in turn: “Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him” (verse 23).

Then the end, when Christ hands over the kingdom to God the Father, after destroying every rule, authority and power (verse 24). “For He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (verses 25-26).

When all things are subjected to him, “then the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
‘But’ in verse 20 turns the whole chapter. After the dark ‘if’ of verses 12 to 19, Paul states the fact: Christ has been raised.

‘Firstfruits’ was a farming and temple word. At harvest, Israel brought the first sheaf to God. It was the first part of the crop, and the sign that the rest would follow. Christ's rising is the first part of the great harvest. Those who belong to him will follow.

‘As in Adam all die’ takes up the comparison Paul also makes in Romans 5. Adam stands at the head of humanity under death. Christ stands at the head of a new humanity, raised to life. The notes on Romans 5 say more, including the views Christians hold on Adam and human origins; these notes take no position on those details.

There is an order: Christ first, then his people at his coming, then the end. Paul calls death ‘the last enemy’. Death is not a friend or a natural door. It is an enemy, and it will be destroyed.

Verse 28 is deep water. The Son hands the kingdom to the Father, and ‘will be made subject’ to him, ‘so that God may be all in all’. This does not make the Son less than God. The church confesses the Son as fully God with the Father. Many read this of the Son's work as the one sent: when his mission is complete, he gives the finished kingdom to the Father, in the same love and willing obedience he showed in his life.
passages.ot:
Firstfruits come from the Law: “you are to bring to the priest a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest” (Leviticus 23:10), and the priest waved it before the LORD “on the day after the Sabbath” (Leviticus 23:11). Christ rose on the first day of the week.

‘Death came through a man’ points to Genesis: “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19).

Paul quotes two psalms. ‘He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet’ echoes a psalm: “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet” (Psalm 110:1). And “God has put everything under His feet” (verse 27) comes from Psalm 8: “You have placed everything under his feet” (Psalm 8:6). That psalm spoke of humanity's place over creation. Paul says it is fulfilled in Christ, the true man.
passages.hard:
Does ‘in Christ all will be made alive’ (verse 22), or ‘God all in all’ (verse 28), mean that every person will in the end be saved?

Christians read these words in different ways, as they read ‘all’ in Romans 5:18 and ‘everyone’ in Romans 11:32. Christian universalists take ‘all’ in the same full sense on both sides: as all died in Adam, so all will finally be made alive in Christ, and God will be all in all with no one left outside. Some Christians, from early times to today, have held or hoped for this; most churches have not taught it.

Many other readers note verse 23: ‘those who belong to Him’. On this reading, ‘all will be made alive’ means all who are in Christ, just as all who are in Adam die. Some add that ‘made alive’ here means raised to the life of Christ's people, not merely raised. Reformed readers often say the ‘all’ are those God has given to Christ; Arminian and Wesleyan readers that the life is offered to all and received by faith.

These notes do not choose between those readings. What the creeds bind is that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and that there is a life of the world to come. The notes on Romans 5 and 11 set out the readings more fully, and the site's Honest Answer, ‘Is hell forever, or does it end?’, weighs the question.
passages.asks: Paul calls death an enemy, and says it will be destroyed. Ask how you think of death: as the end, as a natural door, or as an enemy Christ has already beaten. And ask what it would change to live this week as someone who belongs to the firstfruits' harvest.

passages.t: ‘Baptized for the dead’, and ‘Let us eat and drink’
passages.happening:
“If these things are not so, what will those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized for them?” (verse 29).

And why does Paul put himself in danger every hour (verse 30)? “I face death every day” (verse 31). “If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus for human motives, what did I gain? If the dead are not raised, ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die’” (verse 32).

“Do not be deceived: ‘Bad company corrupts good character’” (verse 33). “Sober up as you ought, and stop sinning; for some of you are ignorant of God. I say this to your shame” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Paul gives two arguments from how people live. First, what some in Corinth were doing: being baptized ‘for the dead’. Second, what he himself was doing: risking his life every day. Both make sense only if the dead will be raised.

‘Wild beasts in Ephesus’ is read in two ways. Some think Paul means it literally, that he was put in the arena. Many think he means it as a picture of fierce enemies, since Acts tells of a riot against him in Ephesus (Acts 19:23-41), and he wrote later of a danger there so great that “we despaired even of life” (2 Corinthians 1:8). No one can be sure.

‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die’ is what life looks like if death is the end. Paul quotes Isaiah. If there is no resurrection, why not live for pleasure?

‘Bad company corrupts good character’ is a line found in the Greek comic playwright Menander, and it had probably become a common saying. Paul uses it as a warning: those who deny the resurrection will drag the church's life down with them.
passages.ot:
Paul's ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die’ quotes Isaiah. When Jerusalem was in danger, God called his people to weep and mourn (Isaiah 22:12). Instead they feasted, saying, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!” (Isaiah 22:13). They feasted as if there were no God to face.

The Old Testament knew the despair of life without hope beyond the grave, and set against it trust in God: “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26).
passages.hard:
What does ‘baptized for the dead’ (verse 29) mean? The book page lists this among the letter's hard passages, and it is one of the most puzzling verses in the Bible.

The honest answer is that no one knows for certain what the practice was. Readers have offered many explanations. The plainest reading is that some in Corinth were being baptized on behalf of people who had died, perhaps believers or relatives who died before they were baptized. Others think it means people were baptized for the sake of the dead: coming to faith in order to be reunited with believing loved ones who had died. There are other suggestions too.

Notice what Paul does and does not do. He says ‘those who’ are baptized, not ‘we’. He does not command the practice or praise it. He mentions it only to show that it makes no sense without a resurrection. No other passage in the Bible speaks of it.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints performs baptisms in its temples on behalf of people who have died, usually members' own ancestors, and points to this verse; it teaches that the dead person is free to accept or reject the baptism. These notes describe that practice with respect. Other churches do not find such a practice taught here, since Paul neither commends nor commands it, and they do not baptize for the dead.

Because its meaning is uncertain, most churches hold that no doctrine or practice should be built on this verse alone. Paul's point is clear: the resurrection is the hope that gives meaning to what believers do.
passages.asks: Paul says that if there is no resurrection, the honest response is ‘let us eat and drink’. Ask whether your life looks like it is lived for this life only. And ask who your ‘company’ is: whose way of seeing the world is shaping yours.

passages.t: ‘What kind of body?’ The seed and the harvest
passages.happening:
“But someone will ask, ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?’” (verse 35).

Paul answers with a seed. What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. You do not sow the body that will be, but a bare seed, of wheat or something else. God gives it a body as he has designed (verses 36-38). There are different kinds of flesh, and different kinds of glory: the sun, the moon, the stars (verses 39-41).

“So will it be with the resurrection of the dead: What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (verses 42-44).

“So it is written: ‘The first man Adam became a living being;’ the last Adam a life-giving spirit” (verse 45). “And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man” (verse 49).
passages.hearers:
The question in verse 35 may have been a mocking one. A body that has rotted in the ground: how can that live again? Paul calls the question foolish, but he answers it.

His answer is a seed. Everyone in Corinth had seen a grain of wheat sown in the ground. The seed seems to die. What grows is the same life, yet far greater than the seed. You could not guess the plant from looking at the seed. So it is with the body that will be raised. It is truly the same person, and yet transformed.

Four pairs follow. Perishable, imperishable. Dishonour, glory. Weakness, power. Natural, spiritual. Every pair says the same thing: the body that dies is the body that will be raised, but changed beyond what we can now picture.

Paul's ‘first man’ and ‘last Adam’ return to the comparison of verses 21 and 22. Adam received life from God. Christ, risen, gives life. We bear Adam's likeness now, made of dust. We will bear Christ's likeness then.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes Genesis: “Then the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being” (Genesis 2:7). He adds ‘first’ and ‘Adam’, and then gives his own second half: ‘the last Adam a life-giving spirit’. The first man received the breath of life. The last Adam gives it.

The seed picture recalls Jesus: “unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). And the glory of sun, moon and stars recalls the God who made them all, “the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night” (Genesis 1:16).
passages.hard:
Does ‘a spiritual body’ (verse 44) mean a body that is not physical, a ghost or a spirit without flesh?

No. These notes say so plainly. Paul does not say the dead will be raised as spirits. He says a body is raised, and he uses the word ‘body’ on both sides: a natural body, a spiritual body. ‘Spiritual’ here means given life by God's Spirit and fitted for the life to come, not made of nothing. Paul used the same two words in 2:14-15: the ‘natural’ person, without the Spirit, and the ‘spiritual’ person, led by the Spirit. A spiritual person is not a ghost. Neither is a spiritual body.

Scholars discuss just what Paul pictures. Some think he means a body animated by God's Spirit rather than by ordinary human life; others think he pictures a body of a higher kind. Either way, the body remains a body.

The risen Jesus showed the same. “Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see” (Luke 24:39), he said, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as he had. He ate in front of them (Luke 24:43). His body was the same body, with the marks of the nails, yet changed. That is the pattern for those who belong to him: Christ “will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (Philippians 3:21).

And ‘flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God’ (verse 50) means our bodies as they now are, weak and dying, not that the body is left behind. They must be changed.
passages.asks: A seed must be buried before it grows. Ask what it means to you that your body, the one you have now, matters to God enough to be raised. And if you are weary of a body that is weak or failing, read verses 42 and 43 again: ‘sown in weakness; it is raised in power’.

passages.happening:
“Now I declare to you, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable” (verse 50).

“Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed” (verse 51), in a moment, “in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed” (verse 52).

The perishable must put on the imperishable (verse 53). Then the saying will come true: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (verse 54). “Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?” (verse 55). “The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law” (verse 56).

“But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!” (verse 57).

“Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain” (verse 58).
passages.hearers:
‘Mystery’ in Paul means something God has now made known. Here it is this: when Christ comes, not every believer will have died, but every believer will be changed. The living and the dead alike will be given bodies that cannot perish.

‘The last trumpet’ was a picture of God's great day. A trumpet called an army or announced a king. Paul uses the same picture in another letter (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

‘The sting of death is sin’ pictures death as a creature with a sting, like a scorpion. Its sting is sin, because sin brought death and makes death fearful. ‘The power of sin is the law’: the law, good in itself, exposes sin and condemns it. Romans 7 explains this at length. Christ has dealt with both. So death has lost its sting.

The chapter does not end with a vision. It ends with work. Because the resurrection is true, what believers do now is not wasted. ‘Your labor in the Lord is not in vain.’ The word ‘labor’ means hard, tiring work. None of it is lost.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes two prophets, each in his own form. Isaiah: “He will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:8). Paul's ‘swallowed up in victory’ differs in wording from the Hebrew as the BSB translates it, but the promise is the same: God will destroy death. Isaiah goes on, “The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face” (Isaiah 25:8).

And Hosea: “Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?” (Hosea 13:14). In Hosea's own setting the words may be a summons to death to come against a rebellious people, since the verse ends, “Compassion is hidden from My eyes” (Hosea 13:14). Readers take it in different ways. Paul hears in it God's final word over death, now fulfilled in Christ, and gives it with ‘victory’ in place of ‘plagues’.

Isaiah also promised that God's people “will not labor in vain” (Isaiah 65:23).
passages.hard:
If you are grieving someone who has died, this chapter is for you, and it does not ask you to stop grieving. Paul calls death an enemy, not a friend (verse 26). Jesus himself wept at the grave of his friend Lazarus (John 11:35). Paul tells another church that believers grieve, but not “like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief and hope can live in the same heart.

Christians have different views about what happens between death and the resurrection, and the details are not all given. What this chapter promises is the end of the story: the dead in Christ will be raised, changed and never die again.

If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. You do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul ends the greatest chapter on the resurrection with a call to keep working. Ask what work for the Lord you have grown tired of, or think does not matter. Then read verse 58 aloud: ‘your labor in the Lord is not in vain’. Ask what you would do differently if you believed it.
